title: O(N^2) Quadratic Time

items.title: What is O(N^2) Quadratic Time?
items.content: Big O notation describes how runtime grows as input size increases. O(N^2) means the runtime grows quadratically with the input size N. A classic example is nested loops over the same list. When you iterate through a list of size N, and inside that loop you iterate again through the same list, the total operations become N × N = N^2. For example, comparing every pair of elements in a list requires roughly N^2 comparisons. This is slower than linear O(N) algorithms but still manageable for small N.
items.explanation: Big O notation describes how runtime grows as input size increases. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt: Which of the following best describes O(N^2) time complexity?
options: The runtime doubles when the input size doubles.
The runtime grows proportionally to the square of the input size.
The runtime grows logarithmically with the input size.
The runtime stays constant regardless of input size.
items.correct_answer: The runtime grows proportionally to the square of the input size.
items.explanation: O(N^2) means the number of operations scales with N squared. This is characteristic of nested loops over the same collection.

items.title: Recognizing O(N^2) in Python Code
items.content: You can spot O(N^2) by looking for two nested loops that both iterate over collections of size N. A common pattern is a for loop inside another for loop where the inner loop does not break early based on the outer index. For example, the code below iterates over every pair of indices in a list of length N, performing a constant-time operation each time. This results in approximately N^2 total iterations. Understanding this pattern helps you identify quadratic-time algorithms before running them on large inputs.
items.explanation: You can spot O(N^2) by looking for two nested loops that both iterate over collections of size N. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt: Consider the following Python snippet. Which statement about its time complexity is correct?
options: It runs in O(N) because there are two loops.
It runs in O(N^2) because the inner loop executes N times for each outer iteration.
It runs in O(log N) because the loops are sequential.
It runs in O(1) because it only prints values.
items.correct_answer: It runs in O(N^2) because the inner loop executes N times for each outer iteration.
items.explanation: The outer loop runs N times and the inner loop also runs N times for each outer iteration, giving N × N = N^2 total operations.

items.prompt: Match the code pattern to its Big O classification.
options: A single loop over N items: O(N)
Two nested loops over N items each: O(N^2)
A loop and a binary search inside it: O(N log N)
A loop that halves the input each time: O(log N)
items.correct_answer: Two nested loops over N items each: O(N^2)
items.explanation: When both loops scale with N and neither depends on the other in a reducing way, the total work is N × N, which is quadratic.

items.prompt: Which scenario is most likely to cause a performance problem due to O(N^2) complexity?
options: Reading a single value from a dictionary by key.
Appending one item to a list inside a loop of size N.
Comparing every item in a list of size N against every other item.
Printing each item of a list once using a single loop.

items.prompt: A student wrote the following function to count pairs in a list, but claims it runs in O(1) time. Identify the bug(s) related to the time complexity claim and explain why the actual complexity is quadratic.
items.hint: Count how many times the inner loop executes relative to n.
items.explanation: The original code iterates over all n × n pairs, giving O(n²) time. The student incorrectly claimed O(1). The corrected version only checks j > i, reducing comparisons to n(n-1)/2, still O(n²), but avoids redundant checks.

items.explanation: This algorithm uses two nested loops, resulting in O(N^2) time complexity. For an input of size N, the outer loop runs N times and the inner loop runs approximately N/2 times on average, giving quadratic growth in the number of comparisons.

items.prompt: Write a Python function `count_substring_occurrences(text, sub)` that counts how many times `sub` appears in `text` using a brute-force sliding window approach with nested loops. Do not use built-in `count` or `find` methods.
items.hint: The outer loop slides the window across the text. The inner loop verifies character-by-character equality. Only increment the counter when all characters in the inner loop match.
items.explanation: The outer loop runs O(N) times and the inner loop runs O(M) times in the worst case, where N is the length of text and M is the length of sub. Since M is bounded by N, the overall complexity is O(N^2) in the worst case.

items.prompt: Write a Python function `matrix_transpose(matrix)` that computes the transpose of a square matrix using nested loops. Do not use list comprehensions or the built-in `zip` function. Return a new matrix where `result[i][j] = matrix[j][i]`.
items.starter_code:
def matrix_transpose(matrix):
    # TODO: implement transpose with nested loops
    n = len(matrix)
    result = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            result[i][j] = matrix[i][j]
    return result

# Test
mat = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
print(matrix_transpose(mat))
items.hint: Remember that transposition swaps rows and columns. The element at row i, column j in the original becomes row j, column i in the result.
items.explanation: For an N x N matrix, we access every element exactly once and write it to a new position. This requires N^2 total assignments, demonstrating quadratic time complexity O(N^2).

items.prompt: A palindrome is a sequence that reads the same forwards and backwards. Write a Python function `count_palindromic_substrings(s)` that counts all palindromic substrings in `s` using an O(N^2) brute-force approach. Check every possible substring by expanding around each center.
items.hint: Iterate over all start and end indices to generate every substring. For each substring, verify palindrome status by comparing characters from both ends moving inward.
items.explanation: There are O(N^2) substrings in a string of length N. Checking each substring for palindromicity takes O(N) time in the worst case, but since we bound the inner check by the substring length, the total work remains O(N^3) in the naive version. The optimized center-expansion approach achieves O(N^2) by avoiding redundant substring creation.

items.prompt: In a social network, two users are considered 'mutual friends' if they share at least one common friend. Given a list of users and a list of friendship pairs, write a Python function `find_mutual_friends(users, friendships)` that returns all pairs of users who are mutual friends. Use nested loops to compare every pair against all friendships. Do not use dictionaries for adjacency lists.
items.hint: The outer two loops enumerate every unordered pair of users. The inner loop scans the friendship list to detect any shared connection between the pair.
items.explanation: With U users and F friendships, the algorithm performs O(U^2 * F) operations in the worst case. If F scales linearly with U, this becomes O(U^3), but the core pairwise comparison structure is quadratic in the number of users. Recognizing when O(N^2) patterns appear in real data helps engineers estimate scalability limits.

items.prompt: You are given a list of integers `arr`. Write a Python function `count_inversions(arr)` that counts the number of inversions in the array, where an inversion is a pair (i, j) such that i < j and arr[i] > arr[j]. Implement this using a brute-force nested loop approach with O(N^2) time complexity. Do not use merge sort or divide-and-conquer optimizations.
items.hint: Every pair of indices (i, j) with i < j must be examined exactly once. Increment the counter only when the earlier element is strictly greater than the later element.
items.explanation: The double loop structure guarantees that every ordered pair of distinct indices is visited exactly once, yielding exactly N(N-1)/2 comparisons. This is the canonical O(N^2) algorithm for counting inversions. Mastery of this pattern allows you to recognize quadratic behavior in combinatorial problems and decide when optimization is necessary.
